title: Matrix Form Ax = b, and the Row and Column Pictures
quickIdea: Every linear system is one equation Ax = b. Read it by rows and each equation is a line or a plane; read it by columns and the question becomes which combination of the columns of A produces b.
remember: A system of m equations in n unknowns is written Ax = b, where A is the m x n coefficient matrix, x is the n x 1 vector of unknowns and b is the m x 1 right-hand side. Attaching b as an extra column gives the augmented matrix [A|b].
Row picture: one equation is one line when there are two unknowns and one plane when there are three. A solution is a point common to all of them.
Column picture: Ax is the combination x1 a1 + x2 a2 + ... + xn an of the columns of A. A solution exists exactly when b lies in the span of the columns, which is the column space of A.
So Ax = b is solvable if and only if b is in the column space of A, which is the same statement as rank(A) = rank([A|b]).
The column picture is the one that survives the jump to many unknowns: the row picture stops being drawable above three variables, but the column statement stays true.

example.prompt: Solve x + y = 3, x - y = 1 by the column picture and by the row picture.
example.work: Column picture: A = [[1,1],[1,-1]], so x1(1,1) + x2(1,-1) = (3,1). Adding the two coordinates gives 2x1 = 4, so x1 = 2, and then x2 = 1. Row picture: the two lines cross where both hold; substituting x = 2, y = 1 satisfies 2 + 1 = 3 and 2 - 1 = 1.
example.answer: x = 2, y = 1. The column weights 2 and 1 reproduce b, and the two lines meet at the point (2, 1).

gateAngle: GATE CSE 1996 Q.1.7 asks directly whether solvability is equivalent to equal ranks, and GATE CSE 2017 Set 1 Q.3 is pure column picture: b is handed to you as the sum of the columns of A, so the all-ones vector is a solution before any arithmetic.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: A is 3 x 2 with independent columns and b is in R^3. Must Ax = b have a solution?
variations.answer: No. The two independent columns span only a plane inside R^3, so only the b lying in that plane are reachable.
variations.why: The column picture makes the failure visible: solvability is membership of b in a 2-dimensional subspace of a 3-dimensional space.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: For A = [[1,2],[2,4]] and b = (3,6), find one solution of Ax = b and describe all of them.
variations.answer: x = (3,0) works, and so does every x = (3 - 2t, t).
variations.why: b is exactly 3 times the first column, and the second column is twice the first, so the reachable directions are one-dimensional while there are two unknowns.

trap.what: Assuming that a solution exists because the system was written down, or reading the row picture as if two lines must always meet.
trap.why: Writing Ax = b says nothing about whether b is reachable. Parallel lines are a perfectly ordinary system with no solution, and the algebra of the same fact is rank(A) below rank([A|b]).
trap.counterexample: x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 are two parallel lines; A = [[1,1],[1,1]] has rank 1, [A|b] = [[1,1,1],[1,1,3]] has rank 2, and no point satisfies both.

check.question: A is 2 x 2 with columns (1,2) and (2,4). Is Ax = (1,0) solvable?
check.explanation: The second column is twice the first, so the column space is the line through (1,2). The vector (1,0) is not on that line, so b is unreachable; equivalently rank(A) = 1 while rank([A|b]) = 2.
